name: Renaissance Periodization (RP) volume training

card.summary: Israetel's MEV/MAV/MRV set-count framework: popular in lifting circles, with no independent trial of the system itself.
card.note: Figures come largely from RP's own and affiliated material.

quick.overview:
Renaissance Periodization is a coaching company founded in 2012 by Mike Israetel and Nick Shaw. Its best-known idea is a set of weekly volume landmarks: minimum effective, maximum adaptive and maximum recoverable volume.

The framework is widely discussed among lifters. Independent efficacy studies of the full system were not found.
quick.mechanism: Trainees begin at a low weekly set count per muscle and add sets over a training block as recovery allows, then reduce volume before repeating.
quick.risks: Higher volumes carry general overuse and fatigue risks of resistance training. Critics mention cost and some diet recommendations; no system-specific harm data were identified.

lead: Renaissance Periodization (RP) is a fitness coaching company co-founded in 2012 by Mike Israetel and Nick Shaw. [1][2] Its best-known idea for building muscle is a set of weekly volume benchmarks for each muscle group: maintenance volume (MV), minimum effective volume (MEV), maximum adaptive volume (MAV) and maximum recoverable volume (MRV). [2][4] Lifters use the framework to decide how many hard sets to do per muscle each week, aiming to add size steadily without overreaching, which supports a bigger, more muscular physique.

In RP's published guidance, a training block starts at MEV, the lowest volume that still grows muscle, and adds sets week by week according to how well the trainee recovers and performs, approaching MRV before a deload to maintenance-level volume. [4] The company's article describes scoring soreness recovery and performance each week on 1-4 scales to decide whether to add sets, hold steady or deload. [4]

Israetel is an American exercise scientist and bodybuilder with a PhD in sport physiology from East Tennessee State University; he built an audience through RP's YouTube channel, which had about 3.9 million subscribers at the time of Wikipedia's last update. [1] RP also offers coaching, apps, courses and ebooks. [2] No independent trial has tested the full RP system as a whole.

chain: Set per-muscle weekly volume between MEV and MRV
Add sets gradually while recovery and performance hold
Steady muscle growth and a fuller physique
angle.text: Lifters follow RP's volume landmarks to progress training volume in a structured way so each muscle receives enough work to grow without exceeding what it can recover from, which supports building muscle over months. [2][4]

paras: RP defines MV as the weekly volume needed to preserve current muscle, about 6 sets per muscle in its article; MEV as the lowest volume that still grows muscle; MAV as the range between MEV and MRV where gains are described as best; and MRV as the upper limit past which recovery falls behind and progress stalls. [4]

One summary gives MRV ranges of roughly 12-26 sets per week for smaller muscles and 20-30 or more for larger ones, with beginners starting near maintenance; these figures come from an AI-generated summary and RP's own material rather than independent trials. [2]

RP's guidance describes starting each mesocycle at MEV, for example 12 sets per week for a muscle, and raising volume weekly, for instance in steps of 12, 14, 16, 18 and 20 sets, according to soreness and performance scores. [4] A deload to MV-level volume for a week, or a new block starting at MEV with fresh exercises, follows when performance drops or MRV is reached. [4] The article adds that temporary causes such as poor sleep or stress should be considered before concluding MRV has been reached. [4]

RP began from Israetel's online content and grew into a team offering one-on-one coaching, the RP Hypertrophy App and Diet Coach App, courses and ebooks, a YouTube channel and a podcast. [2] The company does not sell its own supplement line, according to the same summary. [2] Wikipedia says the name draws on the scientific growth of the Renaissance and the hedge fund Renaissance Technologies. [1]

The Grokipedia summary cites research on training frequency, periodization and repetitions in reserve, and notes that RP-affiliated authors co-wrote a 2022 paper on load progression and muscle size and that RP partly funded a 2019 study on high-volume training. [2] Muscle-hypertrophy reviews describe volume, intensity and frequency as variables that influence growth. [3]

Critics cited in the same summary say some carbohydrate recommendations are high for most people, that templates and subscriptions are costly, and that claims may be overhyped relative to other evidence-based approaches. [2] In 2025 a law student's video criticised errors in Israetel's doctoral dissertation; Israetel said he had uploaded the wrong draft and later released a corrected version. [1]

On T Nation, RP is frequently recommended. One poster calls Israetel and Eric Helms "as legit as they come" with minimal "bro science", [5] another calls RP a "fountainhead" of scientific analysis for lifters, [6] and a third describes buying RP's hypertrophy ebook and planning to progress volume markers on a push-pull-legs split. [7] A poster slowly gaining weight cited RP podcasts on small weight spikes after a meal. [8]
No studies found testing the RP volume-landmark system as a whole. Broader research on training volume as a driver of muscle growth is summarised in Wikipedia's muscle hypertrophy article. [3]

timeline.event: Israetel and Nick Shaw co-found Renaissance Periodization. [1][2]
Israetel completes his PhD and competes in his first bodybuilding show. [1]
A video criticises errors in Israetel's dissertation; a corrected version is released. [1]

lore.intro: RP volume landmarks are commonly cited in lifting communities, including T Nation, as a way to decide weekly set counts. [5][6][7]

claims.claim: Each muscle has a personal range of weekly sets (MEV to MRV) that should guide programming
claims.believers: Followers say tracking these landmarks helps them add volume gradually and deload before overreaching; posters call RP scientific and bought its ebook to apply it. [6][7]
claims.experts: Hypertrophy reviews describe volume as influencing growth, [3] and no independent trial has validated the specific landmark ranges. [2]

claims.claim: RP content is a more science-based source than typical gym advice
claims.believers: One T Nation poster says Israetel and Eric Helms have minimal "bro science". [5]
claims.experts: Critics cited in a summary say claims may be overhyped relative to other evidence-based approaches and that RP partly funded a 2019 high-volume study. [2]
